- **P1 — Butler firsthand, contemporary:** [Oobah Butler, “I Made My Shed the Top Rated Restaurant On TripAdvisor,” VICE, December 6, 2017](https://www.vice.com/en/article/i-made-my-shed-the-top-rated-restaurant-on-tripadvisor/). Full chronological narrative, period photographs and participant reactions. Author is also the hoax organizer; attribute his self-reported observations accordingly.
- **P2 — Independent contemporary reporting and scrutiny:** [Eli Rosenberg, Washington Post, December 8, 2017](https://www.washingtonpost.com/news/food/wp/2017/12/08/it-was-londons-top-rated-restaurant-just-one-problem-it-didnt-exist/) and [The Independent, December 17, 2017](https://www.independent.co.uk/life-style/food-and-drink/the-shed-at-dulwich-was-london-s-top-rated-restaurant-just-one-problem-it-didn-t-exist-a8107791.html). Independent reproductions of some claims; The Independent also consulted archived TripAdvisor rankings and quotes a company spokesperson.
- **P3 — Creator interviewed independently:** [NPR Weekend Edition, December 9, 2017, interview with Oobah Butler](https://www.northcountrypublicradio.org/news/npr/569601017/opening-the-hottest-fake-restaurant-in-town). Confirms key details in his own spoken words and describes actors and dressed-up ready meals.
- **P4 — Contemporary critical industry context:** [Eater London, December 8, 2017](https://london.eater.com/2017/12/8/16747348/vice-tripadvisor-oobah-butler-review-platforms-london-analysis). Supports interpretation of exclusivity/status and the importance of online review signals, but is **commentary**, not an experimental validation.
- **P5 — Independent contemporary report:** [Irish Independent, December 8, 2017](https://www.independent.ie/irish-news/fake-reviews-make-shed-top-rated-restaurant-on-tripadvisor/36389435.html). Confirms setup and one-night stunt, including a pair asking to come back.

## Claim register
| Fact or potential script claim | Evidence | Confidence / qualification |
|---|---|---|
| Butler previously wrote positive fake restaurant reviews for about £10 each | P1, P2, P3 | High for self-reported career story corroborated as a claim in independent reporting |
| The "restaurant" was inspired by a garden shed in Dulwich, south London | P1, P2, P3 | High |
| In April 2017 he bought a £10 phone, made a website, gave a street but not a full address, described it as appointment-only | P1, P2, P3 | High for organizer account with contemporary confirmations; avoid saying today's TripAdvisor verification process is identical |
| Food pictures included an egg resting on his foot, a painted sponge and shaving foam | P1 with photos, P2, P4 | High. The **foot was concealed** in the appealing crop; do not imply diners saw it |
| TripAdvisor approved the listing on May 5, 2017 | P1, P2 | High for Butler's date; independent coverage confirms May listing |
| The initial restaurant rank was #18,149 | P1, P2 | High as reported historic TripAdvisor rank; do not call this a current ranking |
| Friends/acquaintances wrote fake positive reviews | P1, P2, P3 | High; these weren't all written personally by Oobah |
| The first reservation caller was told six weeks fully booked | P1 | Self-reported, directly detailed. Narrate, do not invent an actor's exact dialogue |
| Phones/reservation requests rose; applicants, suppliers and PR firms contacted him | P1, P2, P3 | High broad trajectory; number of applicants/calls is creator-reported if used |
| The Shed became TripAdvisor's #1-ranked London restaurant in early November 2017 | P1, P2 | Strongly supported broad result; **precise date disputed**: Butler says Nov 1, whereas The Independent's review of web-archive ranking pages places its first #1 on Nov 4 and says four days at #1; Butler said almost two weeks. **Omit exact day and duration from script.** |
| He opened the restaurant for one night, with actual invited guests and planted actors | P1, P2, P3 | High. Do not claim it never served a meal or that all patrons were actors |
| Some diners were blindfolded; DJ played restaurant sounds; guests ate inexpensive dressed-up ready meals | P1, P3 and contemporary summaries | High, mostly based on participant account. Dinner was **free**, an important confound |
| Guest experience was mixed: first couple reportedly unimpressed; a different table asked to return | P1, P2, P5 | Supported as Butler's observed experience, not independently measured diner satisfaction. Avoid claiming **all** guests loved or hated it |
| TripAdvisor's response distinguished detecting fake reviews for real businesses from fake listings | P1, P2 | Supported; do not assert the platform intended, endorsed or knowingly allowed the deception |
| Fake signals reinforced credibility and may have colored actual diners' perceptions | P1, P4 and logical interpretation | **Interpretation / hypothesis**, not a controlled causal result; words such as "may" and visual mechanism are safer than "proved everyone was hypnotized" |
| Several credibility signals were *not independent evidence* | Derivation: first fake reviews → ranking; scarcity asserted by Butler; staged actors on dinner night (P1–P4) | Analytic conclusion grounded in this case, not a universal psychological law. Distinguish genuine downstream curiosity from fabricated inputs. |

## The best concrete story material
- **Opening physical contrast:** Burner phone vibrating amid shed/small domestic surroundings while strangers request reservations for a prestigious-sounding restaurant.
- **Food-reveal gag:** Fine-dining egg photograph flips to reveal the photographer's bare foot beneath it; another dish is a sponge and shaving foam.
- **Scarcity:** Only the road, no number; “appointment only” sounds like rarefied access, but avoids unexpected visitors. Callers told it is fully booked.
- **Visible stakes/escalation:** Ranking from #18,149 toward #1; email and call traffic; job applicants and suppliers; a PR firm offers to promote a restaurant that isn't open.
- **Payoff:** To sustain the hoax he opens for one night. Actual diners, actors voicing delight, cheap ready meals, DJ-made crowd/restaurant sounds; feedback ranges from apparent dissatisfaction to requests to book again.
- **Psychological payoff shown visually:** Fake reviews create rank; the rank attracts genuine attention; withholding reservations suggests exclusivity; at dinner, the staged crowd is another cue. The cues look additive, but are not four independent checks of culinary quality.

## What should *not* be in the episode without additional sourcing
- “Everyone loved it,” “every guest asked to return,” “customers paid £xxx,” “there were zero dinners ever,” or exact confirmed date/duration of #1.
- Direct fabricated dialogue, invented private thoughts Oobah never expressed, or official-looking recreations of real TripAdvisor interface presented as genuine 2017 archival footage.
- A strong scientific claim that *social proof* or *scarcity* has been proven to cause any specific diner's behavior in this case; this was a stunt with confounds, not a controlled study.
- Screenshots, music, photos, trademarks or actual voices reused without legal/licensing clearance. **VICE itself noted that TripAdvisor screenshots in the article were mocked up on legal advice**, so label any recreations.

## Open checks prior to publishing
1. Full story owner sign-off on mechanism framing versus satire, comedy tone and duration.
2. Verify whether exact period photo rights/license, depiction of named guests, trademark UI and source-image recreation require clearance.
3. Preserve the nuance that guests received **free** meals and some staged actors were present.
4. Confirm the final VO's facts line by line against this register; file `source-audit.md` records the candidate check.

**Research is good enough to create a script candidate, not a publication-ready documentary license.**

# PSY-A-01 — Differentiated story options and chosen complete treatment
**Status:** STORY TREATMENT CANDIDATE, not founder approved. Based on [source research](research.md) and the account [audience gate](brief.md), not on the old 27-second opening.

## Three genuinely different ways to tell this
### A — The algorithm that crowned a shed
- **Question:** Can someone exploit restaurant rankings without a restaurant?
- **First image:** A ranking dashboard counts down until #1; hard cut to a shabby shed.
- **Spine:** Fake business listing → fake reviews → climb → #1 → TripAdvisor response.
- **Strength:** Fast and high-concept; clean, economical visuals.
- **Weakness:** Ends on a number, mostly attacks a platform, underuses human behavior and the richest payoff. Audience leaves amused, less perceptive.

### B — The restaurant nobody can book
- **Question:** What if refusing every customer makes you famous?
- **First image:** A phone rings; a disappointed would-be diner is told no tables are available.
- **Spine:** Hidden location → fake online buzz → caller refusals → self-reinforcing mystique → crush of inquiries → reveal.
- **Strength:** Distinctive everyday human situation; scarcity dramatized rather than lectured.
- **Weakness:** Could overstate evidence that refusals caused the rise or ignore that the ranking was driven by reviews.

### C — The proof machine (**recommended**)
- **Question:** When a restaurant has reviews, ranking, demand and apparently happy diners, how could the whole thing still be a shed?
- **First image:** A real reservation inquiry, treated as important; reveal the shed.
- **Spine:** Oobah knows fake reviews work → creates a fake listing and fabricated food → recruits glowing reviews → ranking climbs → real interest and manufactured scarcity build on the listing → #1 → must actually open → some real diners don't buy it while others ask to return → trace the apparently separate credibility signals back to the same orchestrated hoax.
- **Strength:** The *events themselves* teach the Psychology/Power/Influence account's desired perceptiveness; provides an earned end after the #1 reveal, real people and messy evidence rather than a simplistic “everyone is gullible.”
- **Weakness:** More scenes, higher runtime than a 45-second microshort. Must be cut sharply and avoid pretending an anecdote is a controlled psychological demonstration.

## Selected treatment C — full beginning / middle / end
**Audience payoff:** Viewers gain a concrete instinct to ask whether many credibility cues come from independent evidence or one manipulated source. Emotion: amused disbelief first, recognition second. Buyer fit remains hypothetical.

**Act 1 — The impossible reservation (setup; ~0:00–0:35):**
A phone rings at a supposedly highly sought-after restaurant; caller told full for six weeks. Wide reveal: it's a shed. Establish Oobah and his firsthand experience writing paid-for bogus reviews. His experiment: make even the restaurant itself fictional. This makes the odd premise causal (he knows the weakness) and gives the audience a question.

**Act 2 — Build a restaurant out of cues (~0:35–1:35):**
A £10 burner phone, a website, street-only address and appointment-only positioning. Invented mood menu with photos of an egg on his foot and painted sponge/shaving foam, executed like gourmet. Real listing gets approved; friends write reviews; ranking climbs from #18,149 to #1. While it rises, real calls, suppliers, applicants and PR offers surface. Whenever Oobah says “fully booked,” the lack of a table becomes part of the attraction. Each new beat either adds a credibility cue or escalates the consequence.

**Act 3 — Reality catches up (~1:35–2:15):**
Oobah faces real customers demanding a restaurant. He decides to open for one night. Bring some diners blindfolded into a garden; surround them with actors praising meals and a DJ providing restaurant sound while microwave-ready meals masquerade as haute cuisine. The question changes from *can the internet be fooled?* to *what happens when someone experiences the real thing?*

**Act 4 — Contradictory responses and the reveal (~2:15–2:40):**
One couple appears unimpressed; another table asks about booking again, both per Butler's firsthand account. Avoid stating that all guests were tricked; the dinner was free and artificial. The final visual reverses the credibility chain: fake reviews → algorithmic ranking → demand → manufactured scarcity → planted social cues. What appeared to be multiple distinct reasons to trust a business began with one coordinated hoax. Last image returns to the very ordinary shed; opening premise and thematic promise paid off.

## Why this length
~330 spoken words needs roughly 2:00–2:15 at a brisk 150–165 words/minute, plus visual reveals, pauses and performance; the candidate **complete episode** should be tested near 2:15–2:45. We do not artificially stretch it to 3–5 minutes or crush it into an incomplete 27-second teaser. If approved, one 15–30-second coherent segment can be used **only** to test animation quality, not mistaken for a finished episode.

## Three highest-risk creative compromises
1. **Too many phone/ranking/UI graphics:** favor two decisive comedy objects and a legible, compact progression instead of 50 generic text notifications.
2. **Didactic finish:** use the visual reversal of independent-looking signals; don't lecture on “cognitive biases” in abstract terms.
3. **Causation oversold:** actual guests reacted differently; ranking date has contradictory accounts; staged actors and free dinner do not prove any precise psychological effect.

**Next artifact:** [full script candidate](script.md), followed by [independent skeptical critique](editorial-review.md) and a [claim audit](source-audit.md). Founder decides whether to accept or change angle C.

# PSY-A-01 — The Setup: “London's Best Restaurant Was a Shed”
**Status:** SCRIPT_CANDIDATE v1 · 2026-10-13 · **NOT APPROVED**.
**Format:** Entire self-contained episode (not a teaser) · Narrator off screen · 2D TV cel animation, pending visual approval.
**Source pack:** `research.md`, `treatment.md`, `source-audit.md`; prior draft and critique in `script-v0.md` / `editorial-review.md`.
**Working spoken runtime:** ~2:10–2:45 at a natural delivery plus visual pauses. Confirm with an actual VO take before committing to a final duration; length not locked.
**Viewer promise:** Understand how several “independent” signs of quality can grow from the same fabricated reputation.

## Full narration (candidate)
A real customer calls a London restaurant asking for a table that night.

The man answering says they're booked for six weeks.

Which is impressive, considering his restaurant is a garden shed.

It's 2017. The man is Oobah Butler, a writer who used to earn ten pounds a review praising restaurants he'd never eaten at.

He'd seen what fake reviews could do. So he decided to try something bigger.

What if the *entire restaurant* were fake?

One ten-pound burner phone. A website. A street name, but no house number.

And one very useful phrase: *appointment only*.

His menu is based on moods. The food photos look strangely expensive. One dish is a sponge covered in paint and shaving foam.

Another? An egg resting on his foot.

TripAdvisor approves *The Shed at Dulwich*. It's ranked dead last in London: number 18,149.

Oobah gets his friends posting glowing reviews. Slowly, the ranking climbs.

Then actual people start calling. One inquiry is for a 70th birthday. Nine guests.

He turns people away.

Suppliers send samples. People apply for jobs. A PR agency wants to represent a restaurant that isn't there.

And eventually, The Shed reaches number one on TripAdvisor's London restaurant rankings.

The only problem now is that people want to *eat* there.

So Oobah opens it.

For one night.

Some guests arrive blindfolded. A DJ plays restaurant noises and little dings to mask the microwave. Actors at nearby tables make a show of loving the food.

The real diners get dressed-up ready meals in a back garden.

One couple leaves looking distinctly unimpressed.

But another table, according to Oobah, asks if they can come back.

To be fair, the dinner was free.

And some of the happy diners were hired to look happy.

Now trace the reputation backward.

The fake reviews helped create the ranking. The ranking attracted real interest. The invented waiting list made it seem exclusive. And at dinner, some of the enthusiasm came from planted guests.

Reviews. Rankings. Scarcity. Other customers.

They *looked* like separate reasons to believe the place was great.

But much of that proof led back to the same thing.

A man with a ten-pound phone.

And a shed.

## Performance / story direction — NOT an approved shot list
- **Cold open:** Start with a recognizable reservation request and an on-screen “FULLY BOOKED — SIX WEEKS” implication; cut to the unremarkable garden shed. **Do not** imply recorded dialogue or a verified location for the actual phone conversation.
- **Setup comedy:** Real hands/objects, one burner phone and cheap staged food. Treat the foot-and-egg gag as a visual reversal, not a generic montage.
- **Escalation:** Let one specific nine-person birthday inquiry be the human anchor; avoid a wall of unreadable mock reviews or fake historical screenshots.
- **#1:** Make the number-one badge a clear midpoint revelation; don't end the film there.
- **Actual dinner:** Differentiate genuine diners from planted actors visually. The free dinner is a necessary caveat; the guests' reactions remain self-reported.
- **Final recognition:** The causal chain visually traces backward and converges on the shed; *no* lecture about generalized human psychology or made-up scientific certainty.
- **Not yet authorized:** Detailed storyboard, image/video render credits, publication, or “approved” asset flags.

# PSY-A-01 — Skeptical editorial pass
**Status:** Critique complete of `script-v0.md`; revised text is `script.md`. **Same assistant, separate critical pass, not an external or independently credentialed review.** Founder script approval still pending.

## Editorial diagnosis
**Audience fit:** The “apparently independent signs of credibility share a manipulated origin” insight does serve this account's aim: help viewers see the hidden influence mechanism. Do not turn the episode into a sermon about everyone being gullible.

**Main problems and corrections, with exact v0 passages:**
1. **Opening overstates an unseen scene and repeats itself.** `"The restaurant is a garden shed"` and `"Then his phone rings... Oobah panics and says... six weeks"` repeats the same event already used in the hook. We do not know precisely **where** he was standing as he took the call. **Fix:** hook is explicitly a caller hearing a six-week wait; follow with the visual contrast of the real shed (not a claimed contemporaneous room position). When we arrive back at rising demand, mention the nine-person 70th birthday inquiry instead of restaging the first call.
2. **The human cost is too abstract.** `"More people call"` does not show an actual person's hope; a reported **70th-birthday booking for nine** is memorable and grounded in the original article. **Fix:** insert it after the first call; avoid invented family relationships, names, or dialogue.
3. **Ending overcounts and moralizes the cues.** `"Five convincing signals"` feels like a PowerPoint principle, and “buzz” isn't clearly evidenced as an independent category. `"Every fully booked phone call made it feel harder to get into"` presumes what each caller believed. **Fix:** enumerate the chain concretely (friends' reviews → listing ranking → genuine demand → false scarcity → planted dinner reactions), then explain in one earned punchline that the ostensible confirmations share a source. Use “could look” rather than proven effects on each person.
4. **Evidence caveat missing.** Guests were **not charged** for the one-night dinner, some diners were actors, and the actual non-actor reactions were mixed. **Fix:** explicitly say it was free, and don't claim diners loved it *because of* staged praise. Explain that one group asked to return **according to Butler's firsthand account**.
5. **Weak duration framing:** the v0 script is a complete arc, not a 27-second teaser, but it doesn't need many abstract filler beats. Draft for ~2:15 rather than forcing it under 60 seconds; once VO timing is real, cut only if dramatic meaning survives.
6. **Potential visual/legal confusion:** snapshots of the original VICE story include legally mocked-up TripAdvisor captures. The script needs visual reenactment labeling and source permissions checked before any archival-looking frame is used.

## Five question Creative OS audit
| Question | Answer / pending risk |
|---|---|
| Why stop? | A highly exclusive restaurant allegedly fully booked for six weeks is just a shed. Concrete contrast has hook potential. Must test phone-screen readability. |
| What happens / why care? | Former fake-review writer tests a fake restaurant; viewers should understand reviews/rankings/demand are not independent proof. |
| What changes? | Listing approved → strangers call → external suppliers and PR act on it → #1 → real people dine → mixed reactions. |
| Is payoff earned? | One-night dinner creates a second reveal, and the backward chain earns the audience insight. Confound: free dinner and staged actors. |
| What to cut? | Second six-week reference, generalized “buzz,” excess list-style moralizing, duplicate setup adjectives; show key objects instead. |

## Approval blockers / open judgment calls
- **Audience promise:** founder may prefer a more sophisticated angle, darker tone or more comic shape. This is only a candidate.
- **Length:** ~2:15–2:45 may be longer than initial 45–90-sec hypotheses; must test pace and perhaps build a complete shorter cut, not arbitrary cliffhanger chunks.
- **Fact check:** full claim-by-claim review in `source-audit.md`. Exact date that listing hit #1 is disputed (Butler Nov 1 vs archival evidence Nov 4): no date in script. Don't call the dinner a controlled experiment.
- **VO:** do a spoken read-through before animatic; exact timecodes cannot be assumed from words alone.
- **Rights and accuracy:** no source-photo, trademark interface, music or realistic reenacted guest voices without careful treatment. Character sheet is still candidate.

**Recommendation:** Show the founder the complete `script.md` for substantive reaction rather than asking whether the hook alone sounds catchy. Mark `SCRIPT_CANDIDATE`, not APPROVED.

# PSY-A-01 — Line-by-line source and interpretation audit
**Status:** CANDIDATE FACT-CHECK, 2026-10-13; not legal clearance or publication approval. Applies to `script.md` v1.
**Primary:** [Oobah Butler (VICE), December 6, 2017](https://www.vice.com/en/article/i-made-my-shed-the-top-rated-restaurant-on-tripadvisor/).
**Independent contemporary check:** [Eli Rosenberg (Washington Post), December 8, 2017](https://www.washingtonpost.com/news/food/wp/2017/12/08/it-was-londons-top-rated-restaurant-just-one-problem-it-didnt-exist/).
**Firsthand interview:** [Scott Simon interview with Butler (NPR), December 9, 2017](https://www.northcountrypublicradio.org/news/npr/569601017/opening-the-hottest-fake-restaurant-in-town).

| Candidate line/claim | Evidence | Status / safe framing |
|---|---|---|
| First real call for a same-night booking; told booked six weeks | VICE “Climbing the Ranks,” first call transcript | Supported as self-reported. Script **reconstructs** in narration; don't fabricate verbatim recordings or locate Oobah in a shed during the call |
| Restaurant was actually a garden shed; prank occurred in 2017 | VICE “Setting Up”; Washington Post paragraphs 2–3; NPR intro | Strong |
| Oobah used to write paid positive fake reviews for £10 | VICE introduction; NPR “On how he came up with the prank”; Washington Post | Supported self-report; no accusation beyond the stated past activity |
| £10 burner phone; website; road name not full address; appointment-only | VICE “Setting Up”; NPR interview | Strong for 2017 historical setup; do not imply current TripAdvisor verification process is equally vulnerable |
| Mood-based menu; painted sponge and shaving foam; foot/egg food photo | VICE “Setting Up” photos/text; Washington Post | Strong. Egg was on foot but the foot was **cropped from the appealing photo** — production reveal can expose uncropped source, not pretend viewers originally saw bare foot |
| Listing approved; started #18,149 | VICE “Getting the Shed to Number One”; Washington Post | Strong as contemporary historical rank |
| Friends/acquaintances posted positive fake reviews; ranking climbed | VICE, Washington Post | Strong; not every review was independently authentic |
| 70th-birthday booking for nine | VICE “Climbing the Ranks” directly after first reservation call | Supported firsthand. Script deliberately does not attribute relationships, names or exact calendar dates |
| Samples, applications, PR agency inquiry | VICE “Things Are Getting a Bit Out of Control”; NPR interview | Strong broad occurrence; avoid specific counts that are not checked |
| #1 in London on TripAdvisor | VICE “Final Push”; Washington Post archive analysis | Strong result; **date differs**: Butler says Nov 1, archive evidence indicates Nov 4. Script has **no date or duration of #1** |
| Real one-night opening, some blindfolded guests, DJ sound, staged actors, dressed-up ready meals | VICE “Big Night”; NPR interview | Strong for events described by Butler. **Do not imply all customers were blindfolded or every diner was an actor** |
| First couple unimpressed; other table asked to come back | VICE “Big Night” creator observations; Washington Post mentions return request | Mixed firsthand observations, not audited independent customer interviews. Narration qualifies the return request **“according to Oobah”** |
| Dinner free | VICE “Big Night” closing paragraph | Supported; retained in script to avoid implied evidence of willingness to pay |
| “Fake reviews helped create ranking” | VICE/independent archive analysis | Supported causal chain in this case, not evidence of exact platform ranking weights. Use **helped**, not “entirely determined” |
| Ranking drew demand; made-up waitlist implied exclusivity; actors influenced atmosphere | VICE and NPR founder account; Washington Post events | **Interpretation**: demand coincided with rank rise; Oobah deliberately refused reservations and planted happy diners. Do not assert all callers or diners were influenced *because* of one specific cue |
| Signals looked independent but were partially orchestrated | Derivation from documented inputs | Clearly **editorial synthesis** serving the show’s ICP; not scientific proof of a universal bias |

## Outstanding controls
- Publication accuracy: second researcher/editor should verify the final spoken narration and exact date nuances. One firsthand account is the source for guests' individual feelings.
- Right to use source images or footage is not established. Draw **original character and UI reenactments**, never present simulated 2017 TripAdvisor visuals as authentic archival evidence. Use no original dialogue/voice clips without rights and ethical review.
- The script mentions an invented waiting list as a **stated six-week unavailability**, not real bookings. Note this in graphics.
- Storytelling review remains a founder gate; quality and length cannot be “unit tested” from a source audit alone.
- Reference status for Oobah's character is **candidate**, not approved; no animation work authorized by this commit.

**Decision needed:** Founder evaluates premise, voice, humor, runtime, emotional arc and value to intended viewer. If accepted, record explicit approval before stage `storyboard`.
